newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAKIA SEES NO SLOWDOWN IN NATO BID.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAKIA SEES NO SLOWDOWN IN NATO BID.

text.p: Slovakia will be ready for NATO membership despite a decision by U.S. Congress to single out three other neighbours for membership in the alliance, a senior Slovak defence ministry official said on Wednesday.
The U.S. House of Representatives in July authorised up to $60 million to help three leading NATO applicants -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- to prepare for membership.
Pavol Hrivik, a senior adviser for international affairs to Slovak Defence Minister Jan Sitek, told reporters that Slovakia would press on with plans to join the western alliance.

"The fact that Slovakia was not mentioned among the three countries should not have a negative impact on our integration process, and definitely not from the financial point of view," Hrivik told a news conference.

He said Slovakia, the Czechs' eastern neighbour and former federation partner, would continue fulfilling its commitments of the Partnership for Peace programme, a special project set up to boost east-west security cooperation in Europe.

"By the end of this year, we will have ready two squadrons of MIG-29 jet fighters and one rapid task force unit fully compatible with NATO forces, as a part of the Partnership for Peace programme," Hrivik said.
However full compatibility of Slovakia's army with NATO forces will take at least 10 years, he added.

Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik last week told the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Vienna that Slovakia deserved to be in the first wave of NATO expansion and did "not want to be a bridge to the East".

Hrivik said Russian objections to NATO's planned expansion to former Soviet-bloc countries also would not hinder the quest for NATO membership of the Bratislava government -- which still has strong ties with Moscow.
"We do consider our decision on integration in NATO as a decision of a sovereign state, despite the fact that we are aware of Russian objections towards the move," Hrivik said.

Earlier this month Russian Chief of the General Staff Mikhail Kolesnikov warned, while visiting Bratislava, that the expansion of NATO could lead to a new geopolitical division of Europe and damage the security balance.
Hrivik however said that no future European security system would be complete without Russia, and should be included in the discussion of the continent's security structure.
Top NATO leaders have said the alliance would press ahead with expansion plans next year and grant full membership to selected former East Bloc enemies despite Russian objections.
A so-far unspecified number of countries from the region is expected to be invited to a NATO summit to start accession talks in 1997.
